title: Emor: counting fifty days (Leviticus 23:15–16)
hook: from barley harvest to wheat, seven weeks counted day by day

segments.voice: Yesterday in Emor, mo'adim, the appointed times. Your line was appointed times. Today, the stretch between two of them, counted one day at a time.

Kids know how to count toward something. Twelve more sleeps until my birthday. Eleven. Ten. Adults do it too, more quietly: days sober, days until the wedding, days since the diagnosis, days until the baby is due. The counting doesn't make the day come faster. It changes the days in between. They stop being empty and become the way there. Leviticus 23 builds that kind of countdown into the year, and the counting itself becomes the practice.
screen: `TWELVE MORE SLEEPS.` → `THE DAYS IN BETWEEN.` → `A HOLIDAY KEPT BY COUNTING.`

segments.voice: After Passover, the people bring the omer, the first sheaf of the harvest; barley, in the rabbis' reading. From that day they count. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "seven weeks shall there be complete". Fifty days, and on the fiftieth, Shavuot, the festival of weeks, with two loaves of bread from the new grain. In the rabbis' reading, barley to wheat. When does the count start? The verse says from the morrow after the sabbath. Which sabbath? The rabbis read it as the first day of Passover, so the count begins on the second night. Other groups in ancient times, the Boethusians, read it as the Saturday after Passover. The Talmud records a long argument, and rabbinic practice follows the rabbis' count. Each night, after dark, the custom is to say a blessing and then the number: today is one day of the omer. Later: today is twenty-three days, which is three weeks and two days. Day by day, and week by week. Miss a whole day, and the Shulchan Aruch rules you keep counting, but without the blessing. The rabbis linked Shavuot to the giving of the Torah at Sinai, so the count became a walk from freedom to purpose: out of Egypt, toward the mountain. This path counts its days too. Today is four hundred seventeen.
screen: `THE OMER: THE FIRST SHEAF.` · `THE MORROW AFTER WHICH SABBATH?` · `TODAY IS ONE DAY OF THE OMER.` · `FROM FREEDOM TO SINAI.` · then, large: `COUNT TOWARD SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're moving toward: a goal, a change, a reunion, a recovery. In your head, say it the way the omer is counted: today is one day. Not the whole distance; just today, a step instead of a wait.
Emor. The portion that commands counting seven weeks, from the first sheaf after Passover to the new bread of Shavuot, day by day.
Your line: count toward something. The days in between are the way there. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until Shavuot, many Jews count the omer each evening after nightfall, saying a blessing and the day's number in days and weeks; some keep a counting chart or app at home.
